subject: biology
title: Unit 3 practice exam
summary: A timed, exam-style test of all of Unit 3: six short-answer questions (40 marks) with full worked solutions, plus 20 multiple-choice questions on DNA, genes, biotechnology, photosynthesis and respiration.
body:
This practice exam tests everything in VCE Biology Unit 3, the same way the end-of-year exam does: a mix of multiple-choice questions and written answers that ask you to explain, apply and analyse. Doing it under real conditions shows you what you know, what you only half know, and how well you manage your time.

## How to use this practice exam

- **Time:** allow **60 minutes** in total: about 20 minutes for the 20 multiple-choice questions and about 40 minutes for the short-answer section (40 marks). That is roughly one mark per minute, which is the pace of the real exam.
- **Conditions:** work alone, with no notes, textbook or phone. A basic calculator is fine.
- **Order:** do the multiple-choice questions (below this lesson) first or last, whichever you prefer, but time yourself.
- **Marking:** write your short-answer responses on paper, then mark them strictly against the worked solutions. Give yourself a mark only when your answer includes the idea the solution says earns it.
- **Afterwards:** list every topic you lost marks on and go back to that lesson. Re-attempt the questions you got wrong a few days later.

## Topics covered

- Nucleic acids, the genetic code and protein structure
- The proteome and the protein secretory pathway
- Gene structure, transcription, RNA processing and translation
- Gene regulation: the *trp* operon (repression and attenuation)
- DNA manipulation: restriction enzymes, ligase, CRISPR-Cas9, PCR, gel electrophoresis, DNA profiling
- Recombinant plasmids, transformation, selection, insulin production, GMOs and transgenic organisms
- Enzymes, biochemical pathways, cofactors and coenzymes
- Photosynthesis, Rubisco and C3, C4 and CAM plants
- Cellular respiration (aerobic and anaerobic)
- Factors affecting the rates of photosynthesis and respiration
- CRISPR applications to photosynthesis and biofuels

## Short-answer questions

### Question 1 (7 marks)

Part of the template strand of a eukaryotic gene is shown below. The first triplet shown is the start of the coding region.

`3′ TAC CTT GGA ATT 5′`

a. Write the mRNA sequence that is transcribed from this section, labelling its 5′ and 3′ ends. (2 marks)

b. Use this part of the genetic code to give the amino acid sequence coded for: AUG = Met, GAA = Glu, CCU = Pro, UAA = stop. (1 mark)

c. A mutation changes the second triplet from CTT to CTC. Explain why this mutation may have no effect on the protein. The codon GAG also codes for Glu. (2 marks)

d. The mature mRNA for this gene is shorter than the pre-mRNA. Explain why. (2 marks)

### Question 2 (7 marks)

*E. coli* bacteria were grown in two flasks. Flask 1 contained a medium with plenty of tryptophan. Flask 2 contained a medium with no tryptophan. The amount of trp operon mRNA made in each flask was measured.

a. Predict which flask had more trp operon mRNA. (1 mark)

b. Explain, with reference to the repressor and the operator, how tryptophan controls transcription of the trp operon. (3 marks)

c. A mutant strain makes a repressor that cannot bind tryptophan. Predict and explain the amount of trp mRNA this strain makes in Flask 1. (2 marks)

d. State one advantage to the bacterium of regulating the trp operon. (1 mark)

### Question 3 (8 marks)

Scientists want bacteria to make a human protein. They cut a plasmid and the human gene with the restriction enzyme *Bam*HI. The plasmid carries an ampicillin resistance gene (*ampR*) and a *lacZ* gene. The *Bam*HI site is inside *lacZ*. When *lacZ* works, colonies grown on a special medium turn blue.

a. Explain why the same restriction enzyme is used to cut the plasmid and the human gene. (2 marks)

b. Name the enzyme used to join the gene into the plasmid and state the bond it forms. (2 marks)

c. After transformation, bacteria are spread on a plate containing ampicillin and the blue-colour medium. Describe the colonies that would contain the recombinant plasmid and explain your answer. (3 marks)

d. The bacteria are now described as transgenic. Explain why. (1 mark)

### Question 4 (6 marks)

A forensic scientist amplifies DNA from a crime scene sample using PCR.

a. Describe what happens in each of the three steps of one PCR cycle, including approximate temperatures. (3 marks)

b. The sample started with 10 copies of the target DNA. How many copies will be present after 6 cycles, assuming perfect doubling? Show your working. (1 mark)

c. The DNA fragments are separated by gel electrophoresis. Explain why DNA fragments move through the gel and why they separate. (2 marks)

### Question 5 (7 marks)

A student placed aquatic plants in water at 25 °C and measured the rate of oxygen bubble production at different light intensities. Results are shown below.

| Light intensity (arbitrary units) | Bubbles per minute |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0 |
| 2 | 8 |
| 4 | 16 |
| 6 | 22 |
| 8 | 24 |
| 10 | 24 |

a. Identify the independent and dependent variables. (1 mark)

b. Identify the factor limiting the rate between 0 and 4 units, and suggest a factor that may be limiting between 8 and 10 units. Justify your answers. (3 marks)

c. In which part of the chloroplast is the oxygen produced, and what is its source? (2 marks)

d. At 0 units, the plant is still alive and respiring. Explain why no bubbles are seen. (1 mark)

### Question 6 (5 marks)

During a 400 m sprint, an athlete's leg muscle cells receive less oxygen than they need.

a. Name the process the muscle cells use to keep making ATP, its location and its end product. (2 marks)

b. Explain why this process allows glycolysis to continue. (2 marks)

c. State how many ATP molecules are produced per glucose by this process compared with aerobic respiration. (1 mark)

## Worked solutions

### Question 1

a. Pair each template base with its complement, using U instead of T. The mRNA runs antiparallel to the template: `5′ AUG GAA CCU UAA 3′` (1 mark for the correct sequence, 1 mark for correct 5′ and 3′ ends).

b. Met – Glu – Pro (then stop). (1 mark) The stop codon does not code for an amino acid.

c. CTC gives the codon GAG instead of GAA. Both codons code for glutamic acid (Glu) because the genetic code is **degenerate** (1 mark), so the amino acid sequence and therefore the protein's structure and function are unchanged; this is a silent mutation (1 mark).

d. The pre-mRNA contains **introns**, non-coding sections (1 mark). During RNA processing these are **spliced out** and the exons are joined, so the mature mRNA is shorter (1 mark). (Adding a cap and tail lengthens it slightly, but splicing removes much more.)

### Question 2

a. Flask 2 (no tryptophan). (1 mark)

b. Model answer: When tryptophan is present it binds to the **repressor protein**, changing its shape and **activating** it (1 mark). The active repressor binds to the **operator** (1 mark), which blocks **RNA polymerase** from moving from the promoter along the structural genes, so they are not transcribed (1 mark). With no tryptophan, the repressor is inactive, does not bind the operator, and the genes are transcribed.

c. The strain would make **a large amount** of trp mRNA even when tryptophan is high (1 mark), because the repressor can never be activated, so it never binds the operator and transcription is not blocked by repression (1 mark). (Attenuation could still reduce it somewhat; mentioning this is a bonus, not required.)

d. Any one: it saves energy and materials by not making enzymes that are not needed; it lets the cell make tryptophan only when it cannot get it from the environment. (1 mark)

### Question 3

a. A restriction enzyme cuts at a specific recognition sequence (1 mark). Using the same enzyme gives the plasmid and the gene **complementary sticky ends**, so they can base-pair and join (1 mark).

b. **DNA ligase** (1 mark) forms **phosphodiester bonds** in the sugar-phosphate backbone (1 mark).

c. The recombinant colonies are **white** colonies growing on the ampicillin plate (1 mark). They grow on ampicillin because the plasmid still carries a working *ampR* gene (1 mark). They are white because the human gene was inserted inside *lacZ*, disrupting it so no blue colour is made; colonies with a plasmid but no insert are blue, and bacteria with no plasmid do not grow (1 mark).

d. They contain a gene from **another species** (a human gene). (1 mark)

### Question 4

a. (1 mark each)
- **Denaturation** at about 95 °C: hydrogen bonds between strands break, separating the DNA into single strands.
- **Annealing** at about 55 °C: short primers bind (base-pair) to complementary sequences at each end of the target region.
- **Extension** at about 72 °C: Taq polymerase adds free nucleotides from the primers, building new complementary strands.

b. Copies = starting copies × 2ⁿ = 10 × 2⁶ = 10 × 64 = **640 copies**. (1 mark)

c. DNA is **negatively charged** because of its phosphate groups, so it moves towards the **positive electrode** when a current is applied (1 mark). The gel acts like a sieve: **smaller fragments move more easily and travel further** than larger ones, so fragments separate by size (1 mark).

### Question 5

a. Independent: light intensity. Dependent: rate of oxygen production (bubbles per minute). (1 mark, both needed)

b. Between 0 and 4 units, **light intensity** is limiting (1 mark), because the rate increases steadily as light increases (doubling light doubles the rate) (1 mark). Between 8 and 10 units the rate has plateaued, so another factor such as **CO₂ concentration** (or temperature, or amount of chlorophyll) is limiting, because more light no longer increases the rate (1 mark).

c. On the **thylakoid membranes** (grana) during the light-dependent stage (1 mark). The oxygen comes from **water**, split by photolysis (1 mark).

d. With no light, no photosynthesis occurs so no O₂ is released; the plant's respiration uses O₂ rather than producing it. (1 mark)

### Question 6

a. **Anaerobic respiration** (lactic acid fermentation) (accept "anaerobic glycolysis"), in the **cytosol**, producing **lactic acid** (lactate). (2 marks: process and location 1, product 1)

b. Glycolysis needs a supply of **NAD⁺** to accept electrons and H⁺ (1 mark). Converting pyruvate to lactic acid unloads NADH back into NAD⁺, so NAD⁺ is regenerated and glycolysis can keep running (1 mark).

c. **2 ATP** per glucose, compared with **about 30–32 ATP** for aerobic respiration. (1 mark)

## Summary

- Spend about one minute per mark and answer in full sentences that use key terms (operator, sticky ends, phosphodiester bond, NAD⁺).
- Many marks come from linking a cause to an effect: "because the repressor is active, it binds the operator, so RNA polymerase is blocked".
- Show working in calculations such as PCR copies (start × 2ⁿ) and base percentages.
- In data questions, name the variables, describe the trend, then explain it with biology (limiting factors, plateau).
- After marking, revisit the lessons behind every lost mark and retry those questions later.

questions.prompt: Which feature is found in RNA but not in DNA?
questions.explanation: RNA contains uracil in place of thymine. Option D is tempting, but both DNA and RNA have phosphodiester bonds in their sugar-phosphate backbones.

questions.prompt: A mutation changes one base so that the codon UGG (tryptophan) becomes UGA (stop). The most likely result is

options.B: no change, because the code is degenerate.
options.C: a single different amino acid in an otherwise normal protein.

questions.explanation: A new stop codon ends translation early, producing a truncated polypeptide that usually cannot fold properly. Option B is tempting, but degeneracy only helps when the new codon codes for the same amino acid; here it codes for stop.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes tertiary protein structure?

options.A: The linear sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.
options.B: The overall three-dimensional shape of a polypeptide, held by interactions between R groups.
options.C: Regular α-helices and β-sheets held by hydrogen bonds along the backbone.
options.D: Two or more polypeptides joined together.

questions.explanation: Tertiary structure is the 3D folding caused by R group interactions such as disulfide bridges, ionic bonds and hydrophobic interactions. Option C describes secondary structure, which only involves hydrogen bonds between backbone groups.

questions.prompt: Skin cells and liver cells in the same person have the same genome but different proteomes. This is mainly because

options.A: liver cells have lost the genes for skin proteins.
options.C: the proteome is the same in every cell, but proteins are destroyed at different rates.
options.D: different genes are expressed in different cell types.

questions.explanation: Every body cell carries the same DNA, but each cell type switches on a different set of genes, so different proteins are made. Option A is tempting, but specialised cells do not lose genes; they simply do not express them.

questions.prompt: A radioactive amino acid is supplied to pancreatic cells that secrete digestive enzymes. In which order would the radioactivity appear?

options.A: Golgi apparatus, rough ER, secretory vesicles
options.B: Rough ER, Golgi apparatus, secretory vesicles
options.D: Secretory vesicles, Golgi apparatus, rough ER

questions.explanation: Amino acids are built into polypeptides on ribosomes of the rough ER, then the proteins move to the Golgi and leave in secretory vesicles. Option C is tempting, but amino acids are not used in the nucleus to make proteins; translation happens at the ribosome.

questions.prompt: In eukaryotes, RNA polymerase first binds to which region of a gene?
questions.explanation: RNA polymerase binds the promoter, upstream of the coding region, then starts transcription. Option D is tempting, but the start codon AUG is on the mRNA and is where the ribosome begins translation, not where transcription begins.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a regulatory gene of the trp operon system?

options.A: trpE, which codes for an enzyme in the tryptophan pathway
options.C: trpR, which codes for the repressor protein

questions.explanation: trpR codes for the repressor protein, which controls the other genes, so it is a regulatory gene. Option B is tempting, but the operator is a DNA binding site, not a gene that codes for a product.

questions.prompt: During attenuation of the trp operon, what happens when tryptophan levels in the cell are low?

options.A: The ribosome moves quickly, regions 3 and 4 pair and transcription stops.
options.B: The repressor binds the leader sequence.
options.C: RNA polymerase cannot bind the promoter.
options.D: The ribosome stalls at the trp codons, regions 2 and 3 pair, and transcription continues.

questions.explanation: With little tryptophan-carrying tRNA, the ribosome stalls in region 1, leaving region 2 free to pair with region 3. This anti-terminator prevents the 3–4 terminator, so RNA polymerase continues. Option A describes high tryptophan.

questions.prompt: A restriction enzyme cuts a 6000 base pair circular plasmid at two sites. How many fragments are produced?
questions.explanation: Cutting a circle at two points gives two pieces. Option C is tempting because cutting a linear molecule twice gives three fragments, but a circular plasmid has no free ends.

questions.prompt: Which statement about CRISPR-Cas9 is correct?

options.A: The guide RNA is complementary to the target DNA and directs Cas9 to cut it.
options.B: Cas9 recognises its target without any RNA.
options.D: CRISPR-Cas9 was first discovered as a defence system in humans.

questions.explanation: The sgRNA base-pairs with the target sequence (next to a PAM), and Cas9 cuts both strands there. Option D is tempting because the tool is used in human research, but CRISPR originated as a bacterial defence against viruses.

questions.prompt: In a paternity test, a child has STR bands at 150 bp and 210 bp. The mother has bands at 150 bp and 180 bp. Which man could be the biological father?
questions.explanation: The child's 150 bp band can come from the mother, so the 210 bp band must come from the father. Only Man 3 has 210 bp. Option A is tempting because he matches the mother, but he has no 210 bp band.

questions.prompt: Which method could be used to help bacteria take up recombinant plasmids?
questions.explanation: A sudden temperature change (heat shock) or electroporation makes the cell membrane more permeable so plasmids can enter. Option D is tempting, but replica plating is used afterwards to select bacteria, not to transform them.

questions.prompt: A GMO that is not transgenic would be

options.A: a bacterium carrying the human insulin gene.
options.B: Bt cotton containing a bacterial toxin gene.
options.C: a crop plant in which one of its own genes has been switched off using CRISPR-Cas9.
options.D: a goat that produces a spider silk protein.

questions.explanation: Knocking out the plant's own gene changes its DNA by gene technology without adding DNA from another species, so it is a GMO but not transgenic. Options A, B and D all contain genes from another species.

questions.prompt: Which statement about coenzymes is correct?

options.A: They are proteins that act as enzymes.
options.B: They are inorganic ions such as Mg²⁺.
options.C: They are used up in each reaction and must be replaced.
options.D: They are organic molecules that carry energy, electrons or protons between reactions.

questions.explanation: Coenzymes such as ATP, NADH and FADH₂ are organic and shuttle between loaded and unloaded forms. Option B is tempting, but Mg²⁺ is an inorganic cofactor, not a coenzyme. Option C is wrong because coenzymes are recycled.

questions.prompt: In the pathway W → X → Y → Z, each arrow is catalysed by a different enzyme. A drug inhibits the enzyme that converts X to Y. What is expected?

options.A: X builds up and Y and Z decrease.
options.B: W and X decrease and Z builds up.
options.D: Y builds up because it cannot be converted to Z.

questions.explanation: Blocking X → Y stops X being used, so X accumulates, and less Y (and therefore Z) is made. Option C is tempting, but Y is also directly affected because it is the product of the blocked step.

questions.prompt: Which row correctly matches a stage of photosynthesis with its location and a product?
questions.explanation: The light-dependent stage occurs on the thylakoid membranes and produces ATP, NADPH and O₂. Option D is tempting because the Calvin cycle is in the stroma, but it uses ATP and returns ADP + Pi; it does not produce ATP.

questions.prompt: Why do C4 plants such as maize lose much less energy to photorespiration than C3 plants on hot days?

options.B: They open their stomata only at night.
options.D: They concentrate CO₂ around Rubisco in bundle sheath cells, so Rubisco rarely binds O₂.

questions.explanation: PEP carboxylase in mesophyll cells captures CO₂ into a 4-carbon compound that releases CO₂ in the bundle sheath, keeping CO₂ high around Rubisco. Option B describes CAM plants, which separate the steps in time. C4 plants still have normal Rubisco.

questions.prompt: Where are most of the CO₂ molecules produced in aerobic respiration released?

options.B: Mitochondrial matrix, during the link step and Krebs cycle
options.C: Cristae, during the electron transport chain

questions.explanation: All six carbons of glucose leave as CO₂ during pyruvate conversion and the Krebs cycle in the matrix. Option C is tempting because the ETC is where most ATP is made, but it produces water, not CO₂. Glycolysis releases no CO₂.

questions.prompt: Yeast is grown in a sealed flask with glucose. After the oxygen is used up, which change would be measured?

options.C: Ethanol starts to accumulate and CO₂ continues to be produced.

questions.explanation: Without oxygen, yeast ferments glucose into ethanol and CO₂, so CO₂ keeps being made and ethanol builds up. Option B is tempting, but lactic acid fermentation happens in animal cells, not yeast. ATP per glucose falls to 2.

questions.prompt: The rate of an enzyme-controlled pathway was measured from 10 °C to 60 °C. It rose to a peak at 37 °C then fell sharply. Which explanation for the fall above 37 °C is best?

options.A: Molecules move more slowly, so collisions are less frequent.
options.B: Enzymes are denatured: the active site changes shape so the substrate can no longer bind.
options.C: The enzyme runs out of coenzymes at high temperature.
options.D: The substrate is denatured, so the enzyme cannot recognise it.

questions.explanation: Above the optimum, heat breaks the bonds holding the enzyme's tertiary structure, changing the active site so substrate no longer fits. Option A is wrong because molecules move faster at higher temperatures; that explains the rise, not the fall.
